Anyone may propose a new category, a change to an existing one, or a correction. Open an issue in the ACE repository describing the RIV, the criteria that would have to be met, the evidence that would show them, and the unit of counting, or write to contact@auditclinicalevidence.org. Accepted changes appear in the version history at the end of this page.

title: Research Integrity Violations
text:
Section 1: Authorship and Publication

RIV 1.1: Guest, Honorary, or Gift Authorship
Authorship is granted to individuals who have not made a substantial intellectual contribution to the research.

Criteria

an individual is listed as an author of the article;
the public record shows that the individual made no substantial contribution to the conception or design of the work, the acquisition or analysis of the data, or the drafting of the manuscript; and
no contribution statement or other disclosure in the article accounts for the authorship.

Typical evidence contribution statements that assign no substantive role to an author; authors whose stated expertise or institution has no connection to the work; authorship patterns that change across closely related papers without explanation.
Counting One instance per author credited without a substantial contribution, in each article.



RIV 1.2: Ghost Authorship
Individuals who participated substantially in the research, data analysis, or manuscript drafting are absent from the author byline and the acknowledgments.

Criteria

an individual made a substantial contribution to the research, the analysis, or the drafting of the manuscript, as shown by the public record (for example, a registration, protocol, funding record, preprint, or disclosure);
the individual is neither listed as an author nor named in the acknowledgments; and
the article does not disclose the omission or give a reason for it.

Typical evidence acknowledged or externally documented contributors (for example, in a registration, protocol, funding record, or earlier version) who do not appear as authors; writing-assistance disclosures that omit the writer.
Counting One instance per omitted contributor identified; one per article when the contributor cannot be identified.



RIV 1.3: Authorship for Sale and Paper Mill Activity
Authorship positions are bought, sold, or traded, or the article is a product of industrialized publishing of fabricated, recycled, or low-quality manuscripts.

Criteria

the article, or an authorship position in it, is shown to have been offered for sale, purchased, or traded; or
the article is linked to a documented authorship-for-sale or paper-mill operation through its authors, its text, its figures, or its editorial handling; and
where the link in (b) rests on the authors alone, the article itself also exhibits substantive findings under other RIVs that are consistent with such an operation.

Typical evidence authors or manuscripts appearing in documented authorship-for-sale networks or advertisements; author additions between submission and publication without a stated contribution; combinations of the indicators in RIV 4.2 together with substantive problems elsewhere in the article.
Counting One instance per article.



RIV 1.4: Plagiarism
Another person’s text, ideas, data, or other intellectual property is included in the manuscript without proper attribution, credit, or citation.

Criteria

text, ideas, data, figures, or tables in the article originate in an earlier work by other people;
the earlier work is not cited at the point of use, or the material is presented as the authors’ own; and
the overlap exceeds what could arise from common phrasing or a standard description of methods.

Typical evidence verbatim or near-verbatim overlap with an earlier source that is not cited, identified by text comparison; reproduced figures or tables without attribution (see also RIV 2.5).
Counting One instance per plagiarized passage, figure, or table.



RIV 1.5: Duplicate Publication and Salami Slicing
Content or findings from previously published work are republished without explicit disclosure and justification, or a single coherent body of research is divided into multiple smaller papers that expand the publication count without adding proportionate scientific value.

Criteria

two or more articles report the same data, participants, trial, or findings, in whole or in substantial part;
the later article does not disclose the earlier one and the relationship between them; and
the later article does not add a scientific contribution that justifies separate publication.

Typical evidence identical or overlapping participants, arms, baseline characteristics, or outcome statistics across articles that do not cite one another or disclose the overlap; the same trial registration behind articles presented as separate studies.
Counting One instance per redundant article, that is, each article beyond the first that reports the same data or trial. A trial split across three articles is two instances.



RIV 1.6: Citation Manipulation
Citations of specific material are forced or coordinated in order to raise the citation metrics of an author, journal, or institution.

Criteria

the article cites a specific author, journal, or institution at points where the content cited does not warrant it; and
the pattern is shown to be coordinated or imposed, for example by editor or reviewer requests, by clusters of self-citation across unrelated papers, or by reciprocal citation among a fixed group.

Typical evidence reference lists dominated by one author, journal, or group beyond what the topic warrants; reviewer or editor requests to add citations that are unrelated to the reviewed content; coordinated citation patterns across a set of articles.
Counting One instance per article in which the pattern is documented.



RIV 1.7: Peer Review Subversion
The independent peer review process is bypassed or compromised, including collusion rings in which reviewers and authors coordinate to approve each other’s work, fabricated reviewer identities or contact details, and the exchange of payment or favors for uncritical review.

Criteria

the article was accepted through a process in which independent peer review was bypassed or compromised; and
the compromise is shown by at least one of: an author acting as the handling editor or a reviewer of their own article; fabricated or author-controlled reviewer identities or contact details; documented coordination between reviewers and authors; or payment or favors exchanged for review.

Typical evidence an author serving as handling editor of their own article; implausibly short review times; retraction notices or publisher investigations citing compromised review; reviewer accounts traced to the authors.
Counting One instance per article whose review was compromised.



RIV 1.8: Irrelevant Citations and Reference Padding
References are included that have no relevance to the text that cites them. Distinct from RIV 1.6, which concerns citations placed to benefit a particular party, this RIV concerns citations that serve no scholarly purpose at all, a pattern often associated with the sale of citations.

Criteria

references are cited at points in the text to which they bear no relevance;
the irrelevant references are numerous or systematic rather than isolated; and
the pattern is not explained by a misnumbered or misordered reference list.

Typical evidence cited works whose subject matter has no connection to the claim they are attached to; clusters of unrelated citations in a single sentence; references to articles later identified as products of the same paper mill.
Counting One instance per article in which the pattern is documented; the irrelevant references are listed, not counted.



RIV 1.9: Trial Registration Failures and Outcome Switching
A clinical trial or other pre-registered study was not registered in a recognized public registry (for example, ClinicalTrials.gov) before enrollment began, or the published report departs from the registered protocol without disclosure, including changes to primary outcomes, analysis populations, sample size, or timing.

Criteria

the study is a clinical trial or is otherwise subject to a pre-registration requirement; and either
the study was not registered in a recognized public registry before the first participant was enrolled; or
the published report departs from the registered protocol in a primary outcome, an analysis population, the sample size, or the timing of an assessment, without disclosing the change.

Typical evidence registration dates after the stated enrollment start; primary outcomes, timepoints, or arms in the publication that differ from the registry entry; registered outcomes that are not reported.
Counting One instance per unregistered or retrospectively registered trial, plus one per switched, added, or unreported registered outcome.



RIV 1.10: Incompatible Authorship or Contribution Statements
The authorship, contribution, or role statements of an article are inconsistent with one another, with the article’s own content, or with those of closely related articles by the same authors reporting the same study.

Criteria

the article carries an authorship, contribution, or role statement;
the statement is inconsistent with another statement in the same article, with the article’s own content, or with the corresponding statement in another article that reports the same study; and
neither article explains the inconsistency.

Typical evidence contribution statements that attribute the same task to different people across papers describing the same trial; statements that credit a role the author list makes impossible; corresponding-author or guarantor designations that change without explanation.
Counting One instance per article whose statements are incompatible.



RIV 1.11: Misrepresentation of Cited Sources
A claim is attributed to a cited source that does not support it, including citing a source for a finding it contradicts, overstating a source’s result, or citing retracted work as though it stood.

Criteria

the article attributes a specific claim, finding, or value to a cited source; and
the cited source does not support the claim, contradicts it, reports a materially different result, or was retracted before the article was submitted and the article does not say so.

Typical evidence side-by-side comparison of the claim with the cited passage or result; citation of an article retracted before the citing article was submitted, without acknowledgment.
Counting One instance per misrepresented citation.



RIV 1.12: Undisclosed Generated Text
Substantial portions of the manuscript were produced by text-generation software without disclosure, or generated text is presented as the authors’ own analysis or findings.

Criteria

substantial passages of the article are shown to have been produced by text-generation software, for example by residual prompts or model responses in the text, by references that do not exist, or by a disclosure made elsewhere; and
the article does not disclose the use, or the generated content is presented as the authors’ own analysis or findings.

Typical evidence residual tool output or prompts in the published text; fabricated references or quotations characteristic of generated text; statements of generation in one version that are absent from another.
Counting One instance per article.

title: Research Integrity Violations
text:
Section 2: Statistical and Data Integrity

RIV 2.1: Anomalies and Extreme Values
Reported data, statistics, or results display extreme or unrealistic values, or distributions that are exceedingly improbable under natural variation, without an explanation in the article.

Criteria

a reported value, statistic, or distribution lies far outside the range that comparable studies and the measure allow, or is exceedingly improbable under natural variation;
the article offers no explanation that accounts for it; and
the value is not attributable to a documented error under RIV 2.4 or RIV 4.1.

Typical evidence effect sizes far outside the range of comparable studies; baseline characteristics more similar across randomized groups than chance allows; variances or distributions that are implausible for the measure.
Counting One instance per anomalous value or statistic.



RIV 2.2: Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets
Reported statistics are internally incompatible with one another, or could not have arisen from a real data set of the stated size and structure. The distinguishing feature is impossibility: the reported values cannot all be true at once.

Criteria

a reported statistical value is not possible or multiple values cannot all be true at once; and
the impossibility holds under every plausible reading of the article, allowing for rounding and inconsequential typographical errors.

Typical evidence GRIM, GRIMMER, or SPRITE failures for means and standard deviations; test statistics, degrees of freedom, and p values that do not match; percentages that are impossible for the stated sample size; totals that do not sum.
Counting One instance per reported statistic, or pair of statistics, shown to be impossible (for example, each failed GRIMMER test).



RIV 2.3: Selective Reporting, Suppressed Data, and Omitted Methodology
Published outcomes exclude relevant data, negative results, or conflicting findings that bear on the study’s conclusions, or the article omits methodological details that are necessary for independent verification and reproducibility.

Criteria

the article’s registration, protocol, methods, or text commits to or refers to an outcome, analysis, timepoint, or methodological detail;
that item is absent from the results or methods as published; and
the absence is not disclosed and explained.

Typical evidence outcomes or timepoints described in the methods, protocol, or registration that never appear in the results; analyses referred to but not reported; missing information on randomization, blinding, or analysis populations.
Counting One instance per omitted outcome, analysis, or methodological element.



RIV 2.4: Data Miscalculation or Erroneous Reporting
Quantitative results are calculated, transcribed, or reported incorrectly. Unlike RIV 2.2, the reported values are possible; they are simply wrong, as shown by recomputation from the article’s own numbers.

Criteria

a reported value can be recomputed from other numbers in the article, its supplements, or its registration;
the recomputed value differs from the reported one by more than rounding; and
the reported value is possible (an impossible value is RIV 2.2).

Typical evidence recomputed statistics that differ from the reported ones; values that differ between the abstract, text, tables, and figures; unit or decimal errors. An error that does not affect any result or conclusion is recorded under RIV 4.1 instead.
Counting One instance per incorrect value; where a single error propagates through a table, the source error is counted once and the propagation is described.



RIV 2.5: Image and Figure Manipulation
Images, figures, or graphical data contain duplicated, spliced, rotated, cloned, or artificially generated elements, or images taken from other sources are presented as original findings without attribution and authorization.

Criteria

an image or figure contains an element that is duplicated, spliced, cloned, rotated, rescaled, or generated, or that is taken from another source;
the element is presented as an original observation of the study; and
the alteration is not disclosed, or is inconsistent with the stated method.

Typical evidence image forensic comparison showing duplicated regions within or across figures; identical images in unrelated articles; inconsistencies in noise, compression, or lighting within one image.
Counting One instance per manipulated image or panel.



RIV 2.6: Data Set Anomalies
The raw data set, where available, shows structural irregularities or improper manual alteration that compromises its integrity. This RIV applies only when data at the participant or observation level can be examined.

Criteria

data at the participant or observation level are available;
the data show a structural irregularity that a real data-collection process would not produce, for example duplicated records, sequences or digit patterns inconsistent with measurement, values outside the instrument’s range, or edits visible in the file’s metadata; and
the irregularity is not explained by the documented data handling.

Typical evidence unexplained duplicate records; inserted or deleted rows; values overwritten by hand; distributions inconsistent with the described measurement; timestamps or identifiers inconsistent with the described collection.
Counting One instance per distinct anomaly found in the data set (for example, duplicated rows count once, however many rows are involved).



RIV 2.7: Image and Figure Errors
Images, figures, or graphical data contain incorrect values, mislabeled axes or groups, or results that contradict the text or tables, without evidence of manipulation (which is RIV 2.5).

Criteria

an image, figure, or graph reports a value, label, unit, or grouping that is incorrect or contradicts the text or tables; and
there is no evidence of manipulation (which is RIV 2.5).

Typical evidence figure values that cannot be reconciled with the tabulated data; swapped or mislabeled panels; error bars or axes inconsistent with the reported statistics. A cosmetic error is recorded under RIV 4.1 instead.
Counting One instance per erroneous figure or panel.

title: Research Integrity Violations
text:
Section 3: Ethical Oversight and Transparency

RIV 3.1: Failure to Disclose Conflicts of Interest
Financial, personal, or professional interests that could reasonably be perceived as compromising the objectivity of the work are not disclosed.

Criteria

an author held a financial, personal, or professional interest related to the subject of the article at the time of the work or its publication;
the interest could reasonably be perceived as affecting the work; and
the article’s disclosure statement omits it.

Typical evidence funding, employment, patents, or consultancies documented elsewhere (registries, disclosure databases, other publications) that are absent from the article’s declaration.
Counting One instance per undisclosed interest, in each article.



RIV 3.2: Bypass of Ethical Oversight
Required ethical review (for example, by an institutional review board or animal care committee) was not obtained, or participants were not treated in accordance with applicable legal and ethical requirements, including informed consent.

Criteria

the study involved human participants, their data or tissue, or animals, in a way that required ethical review or informed consent under the applicable requirements; and
the article reports no approval or consent, or the public record shows that approval or consent was not obtained, or was obtained only after the work was done.

Typical evidence no approval statement for research that requires one; consent procedures that are absent or incompatible with the described population; institutional confirmation that no approval exists.
Counting One instance per article.



RIV 3.3: Ethics Approval Anomalies
The ethics approval or IRB reference given in the article cannot be reconciled with the study: it belongs to a different study, does not match the approving committee’s format, refers to a committee that does not exist at the stated institution, or differs across articles that report the same study.

Criteria

the article gives an ethics approval or IRB reference;
the reference belongs to a different study, does not match the committee’s format, refers to a committee that cannot be identified at the stated institution, or differs from the reference given in another article that reports the same study; and
the article does not explain the discrepancy.

Typical evidence different approval numbers across articles describing the same trial; approval numbers whose structure implies a different year or institution; committees that cannot be identified at the stated institution.
Counting One instance per article whose approval information cannot be reconciled.



RIV 3.4: Implausible Study Timelines
The dates reported for approval, registration, recruitment, intervention, follow-up, submission, or publication cannot all be true, or imply a study that could not have been conducted as described.

Criteria

the article reports dates or durations for approval, registration, recruitment, intervention, follow-up, submission, or publication; and
the dates cannot all be true, or imply that the study could not have been conducted as described in the time available.

Typical evidence recruitment beginning before ethics approval or registration; follow-up periods longer than the interval between recruitment and submission; submission dates that precede the completion of the described follow-up; identical timelines in articles presented as separate studies.
Counting One instance per article.



RIV 3.5: False or Unfulfilled Data Availability Statements
The article states that data or materials are available when they are not, or the authors do not provide data that the statement commits them to share.

Criteria

the article states that data, code, or materials are available, at a location or on request; and
the stated location does not provide them, or a request made under the terms of the statement was not fulfilled within a reasonable time, as documented in the report.

Typical evidence repositories or links that do not contain the stated data; documented, unanswered requests for data the article says is available on request.
Counting One instance per article.

title: Research Integrity Violations
text:
Section 4: Indicators and Minor Issues

RIV 4.1: Minor Typographical Error
Spelling, grammatical, formatting, or transcription errors that do not alter the underlying data, the statistical results, or the conclusions. Recorded because such errors can still propagate into meta-analyses and secondary analyses.

Criteria

a spelling, grammatical, formatting, or transcription error is present;
the intended value or wording is evident; and
the error does not alter the data, the results, or the conclusions.

Typical evidence the error and the evidently intended value.
Counting One instance per error.



RIV 4.2: Indicators of Paper Mill Involvement
Patterns within the article or its authorship that are characteristic of industrialized publishing. These are indicators, not violations: they are recorded only alongside substantive findings and never on their own.

Criteria

the article or its authorship shows one or more of the patterns that are characteristic of paper-mill products, such as those listed under Typical evidence; and
the same article already has at least one instance recorded under a RIV other than RIV 4.2 or RIV 4.3, so that the indicator is reported as context for that finding rather than as a finding on its own.

Typical evidence non-institutional or disposable email domains; author affiliations dispersed across countries with no collaborative history; authors with many retracted articles, implausible publication rates, or publications across unrelated fields; boilerplate text or formatting shared with unrelated articles; templated figures.
Counting One instance per article; the indicators present are listed.



RIV 4.3: Tortured Phrases and Text Spinners
The text contains unnatural synonyms produced by automated paraphrasing (“tortured phrases”), such as “flag to clamor” for “signal to noise” or “bosom malignancy” for “breast cancer”, which indicate text spinning to evade plagiarism detection or generated text.

Criteria

the text contains phrases in which a standard technical expression has been replaced by an unnatural synonym;
the substitution is recognizable by reversing it to the standard expression; and
the pattern occurs more than once in the article.

Typical evidence recognized tortured phrases, identified by comparison with the standard expression; passages whose meaning is recovered only by reversing the substitution.
Counting One instance per article; the phrases found are listed.

title: Audit of Singh et al. (1997)
text:
This report audits Singh (1997), a highly cited RCT of progressive resistance training as a treatment for depression in older adults. The trial has two arms. The exercise arm received 10 weeks of high-intensity resistance training, three sessions per week (n=17n = 17). The attention control arm attended an interactive health education program twice a week for 10 weeks (n=15n = 15). Subjects were community-dwelling volunteers aged 60 to 84 who met DSM-IV criteria for major depression, minor depression, or dysthymia. Depression was measured at baseline and at 10 weeks (post-intervention) with the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD), the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS), and a count of DSM-IV symptoms. The article also reports quality of life (SF-36), self-efficacy, morale, strength, and physical function. All 32 subjects completed the trial. The authors conclude that resistance training is an effective antidepressant in depressed elders.
The trial was one of the first RCTs of resistance training for depression. Meta-analyses of exercise and depression have included Singh (1997) for nearly three decades. The problems documented in this report concern how the summary statistics are labeled and reported. Those summary statistics are the values that meta-analyses extract.



We call a work that cites the audited study infected, because its findings incorporate results that this report identifies as unreliable. According to OpenAlex (retrieved 2026-09-20), 440 articles cite the study (infected articles). Of these, 77 are meta-analyses or reviews (infected reviews). The infected reviews have themselves been cited 12450 times, which measures how far the audited results have spread through the evidence base. The audited study or an infected review is cited by 4 clinical guidelines or consensus statements (see Table 1).

A work that cites an audited paper is described here as infected, meaning its findings incorporate that paper’s results. Infected articles is the number of works indexed by OpenAlex that cite the paper. Two forest plots, the figures in which a meta-analysis lists each study’s effect size beside the pooled estimate, show where this trial’s effect sits inside a published synthesis. In the meta-analysis of exercise for depression in older adults by Cunha (2024), this trial enters three times, as “Singh et al., 1997a”, “1997b.1”, and “1997b.2”, with effect sizes of −3.02, −3.55, and −3.98 (Figure 2). These are the three largest effects in the analysis, where the next largest is −1.34 and the pooled estimate is −0.94. In the meta-analysis of neuromuscular exercise interventions by Nebiker (2018), this trial has an effect of −3.83 and a control group of 19 subjects, four more than the trial had (Figure 3). This entry is the largest effect in the analysis, more than twice the next largest.






Figure 2: The forest plot from Cunha (2024) for depressive symptoms, annotated. The three entries for this trial are highlighted. The darker band marks the range of post-test SMDs that a correct extraction of the article can reach, and the lighter band the range that a change-score SMD standardized by the baseline SD can reach (0 to −1.72).

For nearly three decades, the evidence base on exercise as a treatment for depression has carried this small trial as one of its largest effects. Read correctly, the trial shows a moderate effect, but its tables label the standard errors as standard deviations and meta-analysts extracted them as labeled.



The values in parentheses throughout the article are standard errors, although every table labels them as standard deviations. The article’s own age ranges, subgroup means, and test statistics show this (Section 2). Read as labeled, the trial’s effect on depression is about four times larger than the data support. Of the 24 meta-analyses we located, 19 carry the inflated effect. Separately, the column labeled “Baseline p-value” in the outcome tables does not report baseline comparisons, 8 other reported p values can not be reproduced under any reading, two reported SDs are impossible given their ranges, and one subgroup mean is impossible given its sample size (Section 3). In total, this audit identifies 110 instances of Research Integrity Violations. We recommend retraction (Section 4).

title: Audit of Singh et al. (1997)
section: 2 The values in parentheses are standard errors

2 The values in parentheses are standard errors
Findings in this report are labeled using version 1.0 of the ACE Research Integrity Violations taxonomy (ACE-RIV). A reported value that is wrong as labeled but consistent with the rest of the article once the statistic is read as what it actually is (here, a standard error labeled as a standard deviation) is recorded under RIV 2.4, Data Miscalculation or Erroneous Reporting. A reported value that no reading makes consistent with the article’s other numbers, such as a p value that no test of the reported data can return or an SD larger than its range allows, is recorded under RIV 2.2, Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets. Every finding in this section is recorded under RIV 2.4.

2.1 The labels and the Methods disagree
Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7 of Singh (1997) report the summary statistics for the baseline characteristics and outcomes. The footnote of each of these tables states that the values are “Means and (SD)”. Yet the statistical analysis section of the Methods states that they are standard errors (see Figure 4).

Continuous data are described as the mean (standard error) or median and range as appropriate, except for quality of life measures which are presented as mean (standard deviation) to allow comparison with reported normal values.

Both statements can not be true, but the article reports enough to determine which one is correct.






Figure 4: The statistical analysis paragraph of the Methods of Singh (1997). Blue marks the two statements of what the parentheses contain, standard errors for continuous data and standard deviations for the quality of life measures.





2.2 Values that can not be standard deviations
Beneath the mean age of each group, Table 1 reports the age range, 61 to 82 years in the exercise group and 60 to 84 years in the control group. A standard deviation limits how far apart the youngest and oldest subjects can be. The widest range a group can have for a given SD arises when one subject sits at each end of the range and every other subject sits exactly at the mean, because that arrangement spreads the ages as far as possible while adding the least to the SD. For a group of nn subjects with standard deviation ss, that widest possible range is s2(n−1)s\sqrt{2(n-1)}. A reported range wider than this can not come from a group with that SD. If the value of 1.5 for the exercise group is an SD, even one as large as 1.55 before rounding, the ages of its 17 subjects could span at most 8.8 years, against a reported span of 21 years. If the value of 2.0 for the control group is an SD, the ages of its 15 subjects could span at most 10.8 years, against a reported 24 years. If the value of 1.2 in the abstract is an SD, the ages of all 32 subjects could span at most 9.8 years, against a reported 24 years. The values in parentheses can not be SDs. If they are standard errors (SEs), the implied SDs are 6.2, 7.7, and 6.8 years, which fit the reported ranges.






Figure 5: Panel A shows Table 3 of Singh (1997), the depression outcomes for the whole groups. Panel B shows Table 4, the same outcomes by diagnostic subgroup. Pink marks the BDI and HRSD parentheticals in Table 3, every one of which is below the smallest standard deviation that the subgroup means in Table 4 allow. Blue marks the footnotes stating what the parentheses contain.



The outcome tables can also be checked against each other, because Table 4 breaks the BDI and HRSD outcomes of Table 3 down by diagnostic subgroup, with 7 exercise and 10 control subjects with minor depression and 9 exercise and 4 control subjects with major depression (see panel B of Figure 5). The one dysthymic subject in each group is in neither subgroup. The variance of a whole group (the square of its SD) equals the variance within the subgroups plus the variance between the subgroup means. Neither part can be negative, so the spread of the subgroup means alone puts a lower bound on the SD of the whole group, whatever the spread within each subgroup. For the exercise group at baseline, the subgroup BDI means of 16.7 and 24.6 around a whole-group mean of 21.3 require a whole-group SD of at least 3.87. Table 3 reports 1.8. This bound holds with every reported mean free to fall anywhere within its rounding interval (the values that round to the reported one, 21.25 to 21.35 for a reported 21.3), in whichever direction lowers the bound, with the reported value taken at the top of its own interval, and with the dysthymic subject ignored. The same calculation for all 8 BDI and HRSD values in Table 3 gives lower bounds from 1.31 to 5.51, and every reported value, from 0.9 to 2.4, is below its bound. None of these values can be SDs. Read as SEs, the implied SDs, from 3.7 to 9.9, are all above their bounds.


2.3 Reported p values reproduce only as standard errors
Every reported p value in these tables can be recalculated from the reported means, the values in parentheses, and the group sizes. We recalculated each one twice, once reading the values in parentheses as standard deviations (SDs) and once as standard errors (SEs). Every reported value is rounded, so each mean and parenthetical value may sit anywhere in its rounding interval. Table 1 and Table 2 report unpaired comparisons, which we tested with Student’s and Welch’s t tests. Each outcome table reports a Group × Time p value for every variable, which tests whether the two groups changed by different amounts over the 10 weeks. In a repeated measures ANOVA with two groups and two time points, that p value is the t test comparing the change scores (each subject’s 10-week score minus their baseline score) of the two groups. The SD of a change score depends on the correlation between the baseline and 10-week scores, which the article does not report. We therefore let that correlation take any value from −1 to 1, separately in each group, which gives the widest range of p values each reading could produce. Allowing every correlation can only make the test more lenient. Under either reading the range runs from near zero, where the correlation is close to 1 and the change scores are tightly clustered, up to a ceiling set by a correlation of −1, where they are most spread out. A reading is ruled out only when the reported p value lies above that ceiling, so that no correlation could have produced it. Each range is rounded outward to the precision of the reported value. A reading is possible when the reported p value falls inside its range (see Table 3 and Table 4). Table 5 serves as a check on the method, because the Methods identify its parenthetical values as SDs. Read as SDs, all 8 of its Group × Time p values reproduce, whereas three of them do not reproduce with the values read as SEs.
For 25 variables in Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7, no reading of the parenthetical values as SDs can return the reported p value, whereas every one of them reproduces with the values read as SEs. For medications per day in Table 1, the SD reading gives .00–.01 against a reported .36, and the SE reading gives .25–.46. For HRSD in Table 3, the SD reading gives .000–.001 against a reported .008. For lifting self-efficacy in Table 6, it gives .00–.55 against a reported .59. For the other variables the test does not separate the two readings, either because the reported p value is very small or very large or because the range under the SD reading is wide enough to contain it. ADL in Table 7 reproduces only as SDs, because the control group’s baseline parenthetical value of 0.1 is far smaller than the other three values in the row (0.8, 0.8, and 0.9). It is described but not counted.

text:
3 Reported statistics that no reading can recover
The values in this section are wrong under either reading of the parentheses, so each is recorded under RIV 2.2.

3.1 Baseline p values that are not baseline comparisons
Tables 3 through 7 of Singh (1997) each contain three p value columns labeled “Baseline”, “Time”, and “Group × Time”. The Methods state that a repeated measures ANOVA was used “to analyze the effect of time, treatment, and time × treatment interactions”, which is three effects. A reader would take the first column to be a comparison of the groups at baseline. The Methods name three effects for three columns, so the first column most likely reports the treatment main effect of that ANOVA, the average difference between the groups across both time points, which is not a comparison of the groups at baseline. Table 5 is the place to test whether the column is a baseline comparison, because it is the only table where the Methods identify the values in parentheses as SDs (see Figure 6).






Figure 6: Table 5 of Singh (1997), quality of life outcomes on the SF-36. Pink marks the 7 “Baseline p-value” entries that no test of the baseline scores can return. Blue marks the footnote. This is the one table whose parenthetical values the Methods identify as standard deviations.



We recalculated an unpaired t test on the baseline scores of each of the 8 SF-36 subscales from the reported means, SDs, and sample sizes (see Table 5). With every reported mean and SD free to sit anywhere within its rounding interval, 7 of the 8 reported p values fall outside the range that either t test can return, each by more than 0.2. The exception is mental health, where the groups start and end close together. Reading the SDs as SEs does not reproduce any of the 8. For bodily pain, the baseline means of 56.8 and 72.3 with SDs of about 30 give .14, against a reported p value of .98. For social functioning, the baseline means of 51.5 and 69.2 give .06, against a reported .66. For role emotional, the baseline means of 43.1 and 60.0 give .23, against a reported .91.
The mislabel matters most where a baseline comparison matters. For bodily pain, social functioning, and role emotional, the groups start 15 to 18 points apart and end close together. A reader of Table 5 would take the reported values of .98, .66, and .91 to mean that the groups started out alike.






Figure 7: Table 3 of Singh (1997). Pink marks the six “Baseline p-value” entries, none of which reproduce as a comparison of the baseline scores.



The same column appears in the depression outcomes in Table 3 (see Figure 7). We recalculated the baseline t test for each of its six measures, treating the values in parentheses as SEs (see Section 2 and Table 5). None of the six reported p values can be reproduced under either reading of the parentheticals. One of these discrepancies changes the article’s account of the trial. On the somatic subscale of the BDI, the exercise group started at 8.2 and the control group at 6.5, with SEs of 0.6 and 0.4. The baseline t test returns a p value of .029 (.026 with Welch’s test), against .98 in Table 3. The Results state that “there were no significant differences at baseline in any variables measured.” The somatic subscale is also the outcome with the strongest reported interaction (p<.0001p < .0001), on which the group with the higher baseline score improved the most. A group that starts with more symptoms has more room to improve, so a baseline difference on this subscale bears on the strongest result in the article.

3.2 p values that can not be reproduced under any reading
Three of the unpaired comparisons in Table 3 reproduce under neither reading of the parentheticals. For ethanol intake in Table 1, the reported p value is .34, against .02–.07 as SDs and .56–.63 as SEs. For the duration of depressive symptoms, it is .45, against .01–.06 and .50–.62. For hospital days in Table 2, it is .40, against .00–.05 and .41–.60. All three variables are skewed, with SEs close to the size of the means, which points to a few subjects with large values. Such variables may have been summarized and tested differently (the Methods allow for medians and ranges “as appropriate”). As reported, they are three instances of Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets (RIV 2.2).
Table 1 of Singh (1997) contains a p value for each of 10 categorical baseline characteristics (see Figure 8). The article states that p values for categorical data come from either a chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, without saying which variable uses which. The Results identify the test through three comparisons of proportions reported with their p values: response to treatment in 10/17 exercisers vs 4/15 controls (p=.067p = .067), remission of minor depression in 6/7 vs 4/10 (p=.06p = .06), and remission of major depression in 8/9 vs 2/4 (p=.12p = .12). Pearson’s chi-square test without a continuity correction reproduces all three (.067, .059, and .125, respectively). Fisher’s exact test reproduces none of them (.087, .134, and .203, respectively). The authors therefore used an uncorrected chi-square test, even for tables with expected cell counts well below five, where the chi-square approximation is unreliable and Fisher’s exact test is the usual choice.






Figure 8: Table 1 of Singh (1997). Pink marks the five categorical p values that neither the chi-square test nor Fisher’s exact test reproduces from the reported counts.



We recalculated this test, and Fisher’s exact test, from the contingency table cells reported in Table 1 (see Table 6). Four of the 10 p values reproduce under the uncorrected chi-square test, those for annual income, previous treatment by a psychiatrist, previous antidepressant drugs, and previous hospitalization. Neither test reproduces the other six. For gender (5 men and 12 women vs 7 men and 8 women), the two tests return .31 and .47 against a reported p value of .71. For residence (13 house and 4 apartment vs 12 and 3), they return .81 and 1.00 against a reported .63. Two variants of the chi-square test, the Yates continuity correction and the likelihood ratio test, do not change this. None of the six 2 by 2 tables returns its reported value under the Yates corrected chi-square test. The likelihood ratio test agrees with the uncorrected chi-square test to the reported precision. Before counting a p value as irreproducible, we also tried every way of collapsing the categories of each variable into fewer groups, under all four tests. This collapsing reproduces one variable, employment. Collapsing full-time and part-time work into a single employed category and applying the Yates correction returns .625, which rounds to the reported value. The article describes no such collapsing and uses a continuity correction nowhere else. No collapsing of the marital status or DSM-IV diagnosis categories reproduces the reported p values under any of the four tests.

The irreproducible categorical p values do not affect the conclusions of the study. The reported and recalculated values are all above .05, so under either set the groups do not differ significantly on these characteristics. We count them because they are incorrect. A baseline table that does not reproduce from its own contingency table cells also limits how far a reader can verify the article’s other computations. The five p values that no test reproduces, from the reported cells or from any collapsing of them, are five instances of Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets (RIV 2.2). Employment is described but not counted.


3.3 Training intensity SDs that their ranges do not allow
The Results report the mean training intensity of the exercise group as “78% (SD = 24) of the 1RM (range 45–87%)”. Excluding the one subject who had less than 50% compliance, they report “80% (SD = 10) of the 1RM (range 70–87%)”. Both values are labeled SD in the text (the 1RM is the one-repetition maximum, the heaviest weight a subject can lift once, so intensity is the training load as a percentage of it). A set of nn values that lies within a range of width ww has an SD of at most w2n/(n−1)\tfrac{w}{2}\sqrt{n/(n-1)}, reached when half of the values sit at each end. For the 17 exercisers between 45% and 87%, the SD can be at most 22.2, even with each end of the range rounded outward by half a point. For the 16 exercisers between 70% and 87%, it can be at most 9.3. Neither reported SD is possible. Read as SEs, the implied SDs of 99 and 40 are larger still. No reading of these values is possible, so they are two instances of Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets (RIV 2.2). The Discussion repeats the first value (“mean 78, SD = 24”), which is described but not counted.


3.4 GRIM failure in a subgroup mean
The granularity-related inconsistency of means test (GRIM, Brown 2017) checks whether a reported mean can arise from integer scores, given the sample size. The BDI and HRSD are sums of integer item scores, so a group mean must be an integer divided by the group size. A mean reported to one decimal place can only fail the test when the group has fewer than 10 subjects. Of the 12 such means in Table 4, one fails. The baseline HRSD mean of 13.6 for the four control subjects with major depression would require an integer total between 54.2 and 54.6. No integer lies in that range (see Figure 9). The nearest achievable means are 13.5 and 13.75. The other 11 means are consistent.






Figure 9: Table 4 of Singh (1997). Pink marks the baseline HRSD mean of the four control subjects with major depression, which no set of four integer scores can produce.



Rounding, the scale, and the sample size do not explain the failure. The notes to Table 4 give the subgroup size as 4, which matches the DSM-IV diagnosis counts in Table 1 (2 mild and 2 moderate major depression). The HRSD is scored in whole points. The test already allows for rounding. The Results state that the improvement in HRSD scores in this subgroup was twice that of controls, a comparison that depends on the impossible mean. This is one instance of Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets (RIV 2.2).
The other values in the article that can be checked are consistent. The three correlations reported in the Results for the exercise group (r=r = −0.786, −0.589, and 0.500 with n=17n = 17) give p values of .0002, .013, and .04, against reported values of .0002, .013, and .04. The diagnostic subgroup sizes sum to the group sizes once the dysthymic subject in each group is included. The available evidence points to problems in how the statistics are labeled and reported. It gives no reason to doubt that the trial took place.

title: Audit of Singh et al. (1997)
text:
4 Conclusion
The audited article describes a small RCT whose tables misstate what they contain. Every table of continuous outcomes labels the values in parentheses as standard deviations, yet the Methods state that they are standard errors. The reported test statistics support the Methods (i.e., the values in parentheses are standard errors). For 25 variables across Tables 1 through 4, 6, and 7, the reported p value can not be reproduced with the values read as SDs and can be with the values read as SEs. Additionally, the reported age ranges and the Table 4 subgroup means are impossible under the labeled SDs. This warrants 86 instances of Data Miscalculation or Erroneous Reporting (RIV 2.4), one for each of the values involved.
The effect of this error on meta-analyses is the central finding of this report. The largest post-test SMD the article can support is −0.72 (−0.44 for the BDI). Of the 24 meta-analyses we located that report an effect size for this trial, 19 assign Singh (1997) a value beyond anything a correct extraction can produce. The median assigned value is −2.74. In two syntheses this 32-subject trial is the largest effect in the analysis by a factor of two or more. Four meta-analyses, including the Cochrane review, report exactly −1.75, the value that results from meta-analysts treating the standard errors of the post-intervention BDI scores as standard deviations. For nearly 30 years, the evidence base on exercise and depression has carried a moderate effect as one of its largest.
The columns labeled “Baseline p-value” in the outcome tables do not report baseline comparisons. In the one table where the SDs are unambiguous, 7 of the 8 reported p values can not be reproduced as a test of the baseline scores. Under the correct reading of the depression outcomes, the groups differed at baseline on the somatic subscale of the BDI, the outcome with the strongest reported interaction. Yet the Results state that no variable differed at baseline. The 13 reported values that no baseline test can return are 13 instances of Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets (RIV 2.2). Furthermore, three unpaired and five categorical p values in Tables 1 and 2 can not be reproduced under any reading of the reported summaries, which adds 8 instances of Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets (RIV 2.2). Two training intensity SDs in the Results are larger than their ranges allow under either reading, which adds two more. One subgroup mean in Table 4 is impossible given its sample size, which adds one.
Because the misreporting in Singh (1997) has contaminated the evidence syntheses in this field, we recommend retraction. Every table labels the standard errors as standard deviations. Of the 24 meta-analyses we located, 19 assign Singh (1997) an effect size that no correct extraction can produce. Four of these meta-analyses, including the Cochrane review, report the value that results from treating the standard errors as standard deviations. A reader can only use the published tables as evidence after first correcting them. For nearly 30 years, most meta-analysts have not. In addition, the outcome tables report p values under the label of a baseline comparison that no test of the baseline scores can return. Furthermore, 8 p values in Tables 1 and 2 can not be reproduced under any reading. One subgroup mean in Table 4 is impossible given its sample size. As published, the article’s results have no evidentiary value. This recommendation does not rest on any evidence that the trial was not conducted.
The retraction notice should give the reasons. These are that (a) the values in parentheses in Tables 1 through 4, 6, and 7 and in the abstract are standard errors, (b) the first p value column of Tables 3 through 7 does not report a comparison of the groups at baseline, (c) the groups differed at baseline on the somatic subscale of the BDI, (d) 8 p values in Tables 1 and 2 can not be reproduced from the reported summaries, (e) the subgroup mean in Table 4 is impossible given its sample size, and (f) the two training intensity SDs in the Results are impossible given their ranges.
Whatever the journal decides, meta-analysts and guideline developers who have included this trial should check the values they extracted from it. A meta-analysis that recorded the values in parentheses as standard deviations has treated a moderate effect as a very large one. Such a meta-analysis should re-extract the study with those values multiplied by the square root of the group size, or exclude the study.

title: CORRESPONDENCE
text:
After an audit is published, ACE sends the report to the journal that published the audited work, addressed to its editors and, where the publisher has one, its research integrity office. This page follows each of those letters from the day it is sent to the journal’s final decision, so that readers can see which concerns have been raised with which journals and what came of them. Every address listed below was taken from public records. See Disclaimers for how ACE handles correspondence about its reports.

Each thread moves through three stages. A letter is sent when the report and a cover letter have gone to the journal’s editors, its research integrity office, or both. It is in discussion once the journal has replied. It reaches a decision when the journal has settled the matter: no action, a correction, an expression of concern, or a retraction. ACE’s own recommendation is shown beside each audit for comparison; the decision belongs to the journal.
